name: Summit Peaks Resorts
blurb: Public ski company, six mountains, one season pass. Founder Dana Strand built it from a single hill in Alder Creek and holds 30% of the vote. Alder Creek is the oldest mountain and the town's main employer.

directors.name: Marisa Kell
directors.title: Attorney
directors.motive: A staff lawyer sent you an engineer's warning message last week, and you have not told the board. Disclosing it risks the CEO's trust, and hiding it risks your seat when the congressional committee asks who knew what.

directors.name: Tomas Reyes
directors.title: Labor director
directors.motive: Your union builds and runs the lifts, and a lift operator died on Sunday. A shutdown means layoffs in Alder Creek, and your own pension sits in the fund those layoffs would hit. Your members will blame you if you did not push for safety.

directors.name: Grace Whitlow
directors.title: Fund partner
directors.motive: Your fund owns 8% and your bonus depends on a share price the buybacks keep up. Pausing payouts could push the stock lower, but regulators punish companies that look like they are stalling. Your partners want an answer by Monday.

directors.name: Hal Brennan
directors.title: Founder's friend
directors.motive: Dana Strand is your college roommate, and you skied the first Alder Creek lift with her. She believes the CEO and does not want a leadership fight. You do not know whether to protect her view or tell her she is wrong.

directors.name: June Okafor
directors.title: Community seat
directors.motive: You are Mayor of Alder Creek, where the second fall happened, and you went to two of the funerals. The town depends on Summit for jobs and taxes, you face re-election in the fall, and the town is divided about what speaking for it requires.

briefing.intro: Summit Peaks runs six ski mountains on one season pass and earns most of its money from the Series 7 gondola, a lift it also sells to other resorts. The board has no safety committee, and founder Dana Strand holds 30% of the vote.
facts: Two Series 7 cabins have fallen from their cables in five months. The first killed 18 riders at a partner resort, and the second, last Sunday at Summit's Alder Creek mountain, killed 12 riders and a lift operator. Regulators have closed the model elsewhere but not yet Summit's 41 lifts.

A software fix has slipped three times and could be ready in about eleven weeks, with approval not before August. The cable grip reads a single sensor, and an engineer warned two years ago the design was undertested. The board never saw the message.

The Series 7 brings in $2.1 billion of $9 billion in revenue. Stopping would cost about $1 billion in supplier payments and thousands of jobs, while running on risks criminal claims, a lost license and voided insurance. Nobody inside can say which risk is larger.

The CEO, who is also Chair, believes the lift is sound and says a recall sends the wrong signal. The stock is $380, down 12%, and Summit spends $4 billion a year on dividends and buybacks. A congressional committee wants documents by April 15.

options.title: Stop everything
options.text: Close every Series 7 lift now, halt production and shipments, hire an outside safety review that reports straight to the board, and withhold dividends and buybacks until it finishes.

options.title: Fix and keep running
options.text: Close only Alder Creek and the lifts that regulators order closed, keep building lifts while the software fix is finished, and release a public statement that the fix will make the Series 7 safe.

options.title: Keep building and shield the company
options.text: Keep every Series 7 lift open, continue production, rely on inspectors and lobbyists to set the timetable, and defend the company's record in public.

options.title: Change the leadership
options.text: Separate the Chair and CEO roles at once, form a board safety committee with the power to see all engineering messages, and leave the operating decision to the new committee after a three-week review.

reveal.text: The real firm was Boeing, after two 737 MAX crashes killed 346 people in 2018 and 2019. Boeing cut production, created a board safety committee only in September 2019, and removed Dennis Muilenburg as Chair in October and as CEO in December. A shareholder suit over ignored safety warnings settled for $237.5 million.

questions: Why did Summit save money on one sensor?
The engineer's warning never reached the board. Who blocked it?
Ground every lift or keep running? Pick one.
Should the CEO also be Chair? Yes or no?

press.headline: Summit Peaks Grounds All Series 7 Lifts
press.story: Summit closed every Series 7 lift and suspended dividends and buybacks pending an independent safety review. Suppliers face about $1 billion in lost orders, and a rival lift maker is already calling Summit's customers.

press.headline: Summit Closes Alder Creek, Keeps Other Series 7 Lifts Running
press.story: The company says its software fix will make the lift safe, with approval not expected before August. Families' lawyers said the decision to keep running after two falls will be central in court.

press.headline: Summit Peaks Defends Its Record as Lifts Keep Running
press.story: Summit left every Series 7 lift open and is leaving the timetable to inspectors. Within days the home regulator ordered closures, and insurers said coverage may be void.

press.headline: Summit Peaks Splits Chair and CEO, Forms Safety Committee
press.story: A new board committee can see all engineering messages and will decide on the lifts after three weeks. Investors welcomed the governance change but asked what happens to the lifts in those weeks.
